188.3: This shabad is spoken to one who is wailing over the death of a relative.
192.1: Gur murat: the Guru's form; in Gurbani this is the Guru's Shabad (Bhai Gurdas: the Guru's form is the Guru's Word), not a picture or an idol.
197.1: Bathing at a place of pilgrimage and giving alms at an eclipse of the sun or moon was held to earn very great merit.
199.1: Baisno (Vaishnav): a worshipper of Vishnu, who keeps rules of purity, fasts and worship; here the name is given to the one whose love is with God and who has given up the vices.
200.3: Sitala is smallpox, which people took to be the wrath of the goddess Sitala.
203.3: Rahoa (plural rahoe): a Punjabi folk song sung with a long-drawn call, chiefly by women at weddings; this hymn is to be sung in the ghar (tune) of their chhants.
Sanak and his brothers: Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan and Sanat Kumar, in the Puranas the four sons of Brahma, sages held to remain children for ever.
205.1: Raghurai: the king of the line of Raghu, Rama; in Gurbani, a name of the one God.
207.1: Shiv here means the auspicious One, the giver of good, not the god Shiva.
208.1: Each line takes an item of the yogi's garb and discipline (earrings, ashes, the sect, the food of his order, the seat, the horn, the staff) and gives its inner form. The five disciples are the five senses; the ten are the five senses and the five organs of action.
208.3: The chakor: a bird said in Indian lore to gaze at the moon all night long.
210.4: Diwan: a high officer of a ruler's court, in whose service men worked for pay; the hymn is a picture of service: chaakar (servant), vajahu (wages) and bakhsees (reward).
211.5: Raj Jog: kingship and yoga together, union with God while living the householder's life.
212.5: Chintamani: the jewel that, by tradition, grants whatever is wished for in the mind.
212.6: An elephant, once bathed, throws dust over itself again.
213.3: The staff-bearers (dandi) are sannyasis who carry a staff. Ho in this hymn is a call (O brother) that also fills out the tune.
214.1: Pocha: the wet cloth or plaster laid on the pipe of a still to keep it cool, so that the vapour condenses and drips.
214.2: Shivpuri, Brahmpuri, Indrapuri: the heavens of Shiv, Brahma and Indra, which the Puranas promise as the reward of fire offerings, sacrifices and pilgrimages.
216.1: Robbed on this side: as a traveller's goods are plundered on the road, these deeds are lost before they reach the Lord's court. Aadh: half a cowrie shell, the smallest of values.
219.5: Gaj: in the Bhagavat Purana, an elephant (Gajendra) seized in the water by a crocodile; when his strength failed he called on the Lord and was set free.
223.1: The two paths: in the commentaries, the Guru's way and the way of the self-willed mind; Gurbani elsewhere names them liv and dhaat, attunement to God and running after Maya.
223.2: Sun and moon: heat and cold, harsh treatment and kind alike; to the yogis the words also name the right and left breath channels (pingala and ida).
224.2: Brahma: by the Puranic story, a demon carried off the Vedas while Brahma slept, and they were restored only when he turned to God.

Bali: a demon king who held sacrifices to win Indra's throne; heedless of his guru Shukra's warning, he granted Vishnu, come as the dwarf Vaman, the land of three steps, and was sent down to the netherworld. Harichand (Harishchandra): a king famed for truth and giving, who, put to the test by the sage Vishvamitra, gave away his kingdom and was sold into servitude.

Sahasbahu (the thousand-armed king), Madhu and Kaitabh, Mahikhasur, Jarasandh, Kalyavan, Raktabij and Kalnem: proud kings and demons of the Puranas, slain by Parashuram, Vishnu and Durga, or through Krishna (Jarasandh by Bhim at his side).

Duryodhan: the eldest of the Kauravas in the Mahabharata, slain in the war with the Pandavas. Janmejay: Parikshit's son, who by tradition set aside the counsel of his guru Vyas and was struck with leprosy. Kans, Krishna's uncle, and Keshi and Chandur, his champions, were slain by Krishna.
225.2: Each of these creatures dies through one sense: the bumble-bee through smell, shut in the closing lotus; the moth through sight, in the flame; the elephant through touch, lured into a pit by a she-elephant; the fish through taste, on the bait; the deer through hearing, drawn by the hunter's music.
227.1: By the Puranic story, Brahma was born on a lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel; to find its root he went down its stalk into the netherworld, and could not reach its end.
227.2: Param Hans (the supreme swan): of old, the name of a renunciant of the highest order; the swan is held to separate milk from water. Here it is the one whose food is the Naam.
229.2: Sutak: in Hindu custom, the impurity held to fall on a household for some days after a birth (or a death), during which no worship or rites are performed. The Guru uses the word for the mind's impurity, the love of another.
229.3: The daughter of the ocean: in the Puranas, Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, rose when the gods and demons churned the ocean; here, Maya.
231.1: Seedhe (sijhe): succeeded, their life brought to fulfilment; reedhe: delighted, won over.
234.1: Karhala: a camel (Sanskrit karabha). The mind is likened to the camel that roams foreign lands under its load, ever far from its home; from it these two hymns are named Karhale.
237.1: Dhoti here is the yogis' cleansing (neti-dhoti): a strip of cloth swallowed to clean the stomach; hoti (hotri) is the priest who performs the fire offering.
237.2: Dubidha (duality): the divided mind, which sees mine and yours and loves another besides God; in every line, isu (this) is this duality.
239.3: Akal: without parts (kala), the One who neither wanes nor waxes as the moon does; a name of God.
242.1: Jumla (the total): the closing figure 44 is the count of all the Ashtapadis in Raag Gauri.
242.2: Milk once drawn does not come back to the teats: the youth (and the chance of union) lost in pride do not return.
The friends and the wicked: in the commentaries, the virtues within, which flourish, and the vices, which are crushed.
246.1: In this hymn a wife speaks to her husband, who leaves home to serve another in foreign lands; in the commentaries this husband is the soul, which leaves its home within to wander after Maya.
The closing figure 7 is the total of these Chhants in Raag Gauri: two by the First Guru and five by the Third.
250.1: Bavan Akhri (fifty-two letters): a composition in which each pauri opens with a letter of the alphabet (Ong, Sassa, Dhadha, Nganga and the rest); each salok gives the thought that the pauri after it unfolds.
250.3: Ong: the first letter of the alphabet, here also the name of Ik Oankar, the One God. Sunn (the void): the state before creation, when there was nothing but God.
250.4: Nirgun: God beyond the three qualities of Maya; Sargun: God made manifest in the creation, with its qualities.
251.3: Nganga: for the acrostic, giaan (spiritual wisdom) and giaani (the wise) are spelt here with the letter ਙ.
253.5: Purak, kumbhak and rechak are the three parts of the yogis' breath control (pranayam). A sompaak cooks his own food for ritual purity; an aparas lets no one touch him.
254.4: Punahcharan: a rite of expiation, performed to wipe out the effect of a sin.
254.7: In ਗੋੁਬਿੰਦ the letter ਗ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read gubind, to keep the metre of the line.
255.2: The nalini is a parrot trap: a reed that turns on a rod set over a bowl of water, with grain on it. When the parrot perches, the reed turns over; seeing the water below, the frightened bird clings to it and so is caught by its own hold.
259.9: Vasudev: a name of Krishna, son of Vasudeva; in Gurbani it names God, who dwells in all.
261.6: Akhar: in this pauri, letters, the written and spoken word in which the whole visible world is named and known; in the salok before it, akhar (Sanskrit akshara, the imperishable) is the imperishable Lord, who is untouched by letters.
296.1: Thiti (lunar days): the days of the moon's fortnight, Ekam (the first), Dutiya (the second), Tritiya (the third) and the rest. Each pauri of this bani opens with a lunar day's name, and instead of the day's observances the Guru draws a teaching from the name (Ekam: the One Creator; Dutiya: duality and evil-mindedness; Tritiya: the three qualities).
297.8: Sekh: Shesh Nag, the thousand-headed serpent of the Puranas, held to utter a new Name of God with every tongue. Suk (Shukdev), the son of the sage Vyas, recited the Bhagavat Purana to King Parikshit.
299.2: On Ekadasi, the eleventh day of the moon's fortnight, many Hindus fast from grain; here the Guru tells what the true fast is.
299.4: Panch bhoo atma: the mind, held to be formed from the subtle part of the five elements (earth, water, fire, air and ether).
299.6: The three fevers: adhi (ills of the mind), biadhi (ills of the body) and upadhi (troubles and calamities that come from without).
302.3: Jaani, bhaani, ajaani, vakhaani and samaani are feminine: this pauri speaks of the soul-bride.
305.4: Amrit sar, the pool of Amrit: in Gurbani, the Naam pictured as a pool of Amrit; after the outward bath, the Sikh dips in it.
306.2: This salok tells of an incident: by tradition, a man turned away from the Guru, with his servant, brought false complaints against Guru Amar Das Ji before the emperor Akbar, and both came back disgraced.
309.1: Bahi tikia: (the Guru) sat and anointed (him) with the tilak, that is, himself entrusted (him) with the Guruship.
315.3: Azrail (Azrael): in Islamic tradition, the angel of death, who takes the soul from the body.
315.10: This salok tells of an incident: by tradition, an ascetic (tapa) first turned down the Guru's invitation to receive the alms given to holy men, then, greedy for the large offering, seated his own son among them (to take a share). Panch: the leading men of the town, its council.
318.1: Rai Kamaldi Mojdi: by tradition, Rai Kamaluddin and his nephew Maujuddin, whose fight the bards sang as a vaar; this vaar is to be sung to its tune (dhuni).
319.9: The pods of the ak split open when they dry, and scatter in a thousand silky tufts.
319.11: Nanaku, with the aunkar, is the subject here: it is Nanak, the Guru, who gives the Name; it is not an address (O Nanak).
319.13: This salok speaks to a Muslim in his own terms: Dozakh is hell, and Rasul is God's Prophet, who here stands for the Guru.
321.1: Bhaleria here means bad, evil, not good.
321.11: The commentaries read this salok as an image of the rain of the Name: the earth is the heart, and the grain the Lord's praise.
322.3: The kite: in the commentaries, the mind cut off from God, which roams everywhere yet settles only on the carrion of vice.
322.5: Doha: a couplet, a metre of two lines.
322.9: Khundi: a game played with a curved stick and a ball; kunde: the butts of guns.
323.5: Jajman: the patron whose household rites a Brahmin performs and who gives him his dues.
325.5: The little well is the body (and attachment to it), the five water-drawers are the senses, and the broken rope is the want of true understanding: the misled intellect labours through the senses to draw pleasure, and gets nothing (the Darpan's reading).
326.1: By the Darpan's reading, the last stanza (ਰਾਮ ਰਮਤ ਮਤਿ ਪਰਗਟੀ ਆਈ …) is the Fifth Guru's, joined to tell how this understanding comes; the extra figure 1 in the closing numbers marks it. The Faridkot Teeka takes the whole hymn as the Guru's.

In the Darpan's reading, the donkey and the maddened buffalo are the foolish, headstrong mind feeding on pleasures; the ewe suckling at her lamb is the intellect following the mind, when the mind should follow the intellect.
326.2: Panchpade: hymns of five stanzas. Kashi (Banaras), Shiva's city, was believed to free whoever died there, and Magahar to send whoever died there into birth as a donkey; to break this belief, Kabir left Kashi in old age to live and die at Magahar.
326.4: Tipade Chartuke: hymns of three stanzas, each of four lines.
327.1: Sukhmana: in yoga, the central channel of the subtle body, between the ida and the pingala, where yogis hold the breath; the ida and the pingala they also call the Ganga and the Jamuna, whose meeting, like the Triveni at Prayag, counts as a holy bathing place. Kabir turns these images inward; the Darpan reads the Rahao line as remembering the Name with every breath.
328.6: Kabir speaks of the Name's elixir in the image of distilling: the still, the firewood and the kalalan (the woman who serves the wine); the sky is the raised mind where the elixir drips.
329.2: The Smritis: the law-books based on the Vedas (Manu's and others), which lay down the rules of caste and ritual.
329.4: The five ambrosial foods: milk, curd, ghee, sugar and honey, held to be the finest of foods.
329.5: Nat: the player who takes on every part of his show himself.
330.1: Pade: hymns; thirty-five is the count of Kabir's hymns in Gauri Guareri up to here.
330.4: This hymn is to be sung both in Raag Gauri and in Raag Sorath.
331.1: Thagauri (the thugs' stupefying drug, 61.1) here is the attachment by which the Lord holds the world spellbound.
332.1: By the Puranic story, King Bhagirath brought the Ganga down from heaven to the earth.
332.2: Shraadh: the rite for dead forebears (pitars), in which food is given to Brahmins and set out for crows, in the belief that it reaches the forebears.
Akul: without kul (lineage); the Lord, who has no forebears.
333.1: The six chakras: in yoga, six centres in the body, from the base of the spine to the point between the brows, through which yogis draw the breath upward.
Palita: the fuse that fires the powder of a gun.
333.3: Tanda: a trader's caravan of laden oxen; nayak: the master of the banjaras (travelling traders); jagati: the collector of tolls on the road.
334.3: Kingri: the yogis' stringed instrument, a stem set on two gourds; batua: the yogi's pouch for ashes; tari: the yogic trance.
335.1: The body here is cloth on a loom: the commentators read the nine yards as the body's nine openings, the ten as the senses, the twenty-one as the elements, the vital airs and the mind, the sixty threads as the main channels of the body, the nine pieces as its joints and the seventy-two as its finer channels.

Maho: the mind's craving, which takes the soul off again and again to have a body woven; sizing (pachan): the paste that stiffens the warp, here the daily food; the troughs (kunde): the pots in which the bobbins are kept soaking; the beam (tur): the roller on which the woven cloth is wound.
335.2: Kashi: by the Puranas, Shiva whispers the saving mantra (the Name of Ram) into the ear of one who dies in Kashi (Benares), and he is liberated.
335.4: A monkey is trapped with grain put in a narrow-mouthed pot: the full fist will not come out, and the greedy monkey will not let go, so he is caught, and the showman makes him dance from door to door.
Nalini: a parrot trap, a turning tube baited with grain over water; when the parrot perches, the tube turns over, and in fear of falling he clings to it and is caught.
336.2: Tin ko mandar: tin is straw or grass; the body is a house of straw, set alight by the fire of passing life.
337.1: Dhru: the child prince who, slighted by his stepmother, gave himself to devotion and was given an unmoving place as the Pole Star.
337.2: It was believed that the child in the womb, hanging head down like an ascetic doing penance upside down, remembers God.
337.5: A woman awaiting her husband from abroad shoos the crow from the roof: if it flies off, her beloved is said to be coming. In udahu na, the na is not a negative but a fond entreaty.
338.1: Kabir takes the longing of the milkmaid of Gokul, enchanted by Krishna in Brindaban, as the picture of his own love for the Lord.
338.3: Sindhaura: the coconut smeared with vermilion that a widow took in her hand as she went to be burned on her husband's pyre; once she had taken it, there was no turning back.
338.5: Nand: the cowherd of Gokul in whose home, by the Puranas, Krishna was brought up; Kabir answers the belief that God was born as anyone's son.
340.5: Tariqat: the second of the four stages of the Sufi path to God (shariat, tariqat, marifat, haqiqat), the stage of the heart's purification.
340.7: The lotus opens to the sun's ray and closes when the moon rises.
342.4: Shakti and Shiv: in Hindu thought the Goddess (the power of Maya) and Shiv; the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka read that the mind becomes what it joins: Maya with Maya, the Lord with the Lord, the body with the body. Unman: the state of the mind raised above the world's thoughts and settled in the Lord.
342.8: Bisan (Vishnu) is here a name of the one Lord; the Bisantana, the son of Bisan, is his devotee, who like a child knows him alone as his keeper.
343.10: Khat chakra (the six wheels): taking the name of the yogis' six chakras, here, by the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka, the five senses and the mind; the six directions are the four quarters, below and above.
343.12: The eight elements (dhatu): in the old count, the eight constituents of the body (by the Darpan: chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen and the nerves).
344.3: Twelve suns: the Puranas count twelve suns (the Adityas); here they are the full light of knowledge risen within.
344.7: Vaar Sat (the seven days): each stanza opens with a day of the week: Aadit (Sunday), Somvar (Monday), Mangalvar (Tuesday), Budhvar (Wednesday), Brihaspati (Thursday) and Thavar (Saturday); Friday's (Shukarvar's) stanza opens with the like-sounding sukrit, good deeds. In place of each day's fasts and observances, Kabir draws a lesson in devotion from its name.

The upturned lotus: the heart turned away from the Lord. Trikuti (the knitted brow, 18.2) the Darpan reads as the mind's fretting; yogis give the name trikuti to the point between the brows, where the ida, pingala and sukhmana are held to meet, and the Faridkot Teeka and the Santhya read the line as bathing there day and night in that inner Triveni to wash away sins.
345.1: Stones: the stones of Ram's bridge to Lanka, said to have floated because his Name was written on them.

Ganika: a courtesan, saved by teaching a parrot to say Ram; Kubija: the hunchbacked maid of Kans, made straight and fair by Krishna; Ajamal: a fallen Brahmin, saved when at death he called his son Narayan; the hunter: Jara, who shot Krishna in the foot, taking him for a deer.
Bidar (Vidura): born of a maidservant, a devotee of Krishna; Sudama: Krishna's poor Brahmin friend, made rich by him; Ugrasain: the father of Kans, restored to the throne when Krishna slew Kans.
345.2: Begampura (be-gham, without sorrow): the city is the soul's own state in union with the Lord, reached in this life, set against the heaven that others promise after death.
345.3: The trader is the seeker: his ox is the mind, his capital and cargo the Lord's Name, and the hard mountain passes the lures of the senses on the way.
The knowers of this world and the next: Chitr and Gupt, who write down each one's deeds for Jam.
346.2: Satjug, Treta, Duapar and Kalyug: the four ages of the Puranic count; the scriptures give each age its own way to liberation, which Ravidas questions here.
347.1: Dharam Raj judges each soul by its deeds; Chitr and Gupt are, by tradition, the two recorders at his court who write down the deeds of every being.

Mach is the mortal world, between heaven and the netherworld. The jewels: by tradition, the fourteen jewels that came out of the ocean when it was churned. The sixty-eight places of pilgrimage are the tiraths held most holy in India.
The four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth.
348.1: Niranjan: nir (without) and anjan (collyrium, black stain); the One on whom the stain of Maya does not fall.
Ji, in nearly every line of this shabad, is a word of reverence for God.
ਜਨੁ ਨਾਨਕੁ (with the aunkar) is the subject: servant Nanak himself is the sacrifice; ਜਨ ਨਾਨਕ (without it) is an address, O servant Nanak, or, with a postposition understood, of servant Nanak.

The Simritis are the Hindu books of conduct and law, the Shastras the books of the six schools of philosophy; the six duties (khat karam) are a Brahmin's: to study and to teach, to perform sacrifice and to have it performed, to give alms and to receive them.
348.2: The Siddhas are yogis held to have reached perfection; siddhi is attainment, the miraculous powers among it.
349.1: Kamjaat (low-born) and sanaat (counted outside the four castes) are not caste by birth here: the Guru says the low are those who forget the Master.
349.3: Narad, the sage of the Puranas, roams the worlds singing and dancing with his vina; here he stands for the restless mind.
Taam (Arabic ta'am): food, bread.
350.3: Kali: the serpent Kaliya, whom, in the Puranas, Krishna subdued in the Yamuna. In the Puranas Brahma was born of a lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel, and went down its stalk to find where it began, but found no end.
The gods and demons quarrelled over the jewels that came out of the churned ocean; in the Puranas Vishnu took the form of Mohini, an enchantress, and shared them out one by one.
351.2: The family of the raags: in the old tradition of Indian music each raag has its raginis (consorts) and its sons.
352.1: The lake is the Saadh Sangat, the lotuses the Sants who live in it, the swans the Gurmukhs; as the lotus in the lake stays in bloom by water, so the mind that abides in the Sangat by the Naam. The three branches: the three qualities of Maya.
354.1: Tituka: a hymn whose every stanza has three lines; here each line is a pair of short lines.
355.1: Janeu: the sacred thread worn by Brahmins; kuspaati: a ring of kusha grass worn on the finger during worship.
356.3: Ankle-bells are worn by those who dance in worship. Digambar (sky-clad): a Jain ascetic who goes naked; the Jains hold to ahimsa, harming no living being.
356.4: Each of the four stanzas of this shabad is followed by a Rahao line of its own.
357.3: The saravarra is a lake, here the world: its water is the fire of craving and its mire attachment. Pankaj here is not the lotus but the mire (pank).
Bhaile and dubiale are past forms of an eastern dialect: has come to be, have drowned.
357.4: The six houses are the six schools (darshanas) of Indian philosophy: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta; the six teachers are their founders: Gautama, Kanada, Kapila, Patanjali, Jaimini and Vyasa.

The units of time: a visa is the time of fifteen blinks of the eye, fifteen visas make a chasa; a ghari is about twenty-four minutes and a pahar about three hours; the lunar days (thitis) are the dates of the moon's calendar.
358.2: Lokee and chhamichhari: by the Darpan, the gods and the forefathers (pitars), to whom pinds are offered in the rites for the dead (149.7). A ratti is a very small weight.
359.1: In this shabad the body speaks as a bride: the five friends are the five senses, and the one husband is the soul, which must leave the body.
359.3: Satranj here, by the Darpan, is the game of chaupar (113.1), in which a piece that does not reach home stays raw. Bandi (submission to God's will) and banda (his servant, a man) are a play on one word.
359.4: Bharthari: a famous yogi of Gorakhnath's order, by tradition a king of Ujjain who gave up his throne for yoga; yogis also took the names of their famous masters.
The sammia (bairagan) is the wooden rest on which a yogi leans his arms in meditation; the pat (patra) is the begging bowl; Atit (the detached) is a name for an order of renunciants.
360.1: Liquor is distilled from molasses set to ferment with dhava (mahua) flowers and kikar bark (kas); the pocha is the wet cloth that cools the pipe, so that the vapour drips as spirit. Some yogis drank liquor for their trances.
360.2: Khurasan: to the people of Hindustan, the lands west of the Indus; the Mughal is Babur, who invaded Hindustan from there.
360.3: Darshan is sight, and also a school of thought, a way of seeing the truth. Here the Guru's darshan is both the sight of the Guru and the path he shows.
362.1: The root is the Lord, the source of all; the branch is what grows from him: Maya, or the worship of other gods in place of him.
362.3: Lala: a slave bought by his master; here the servant who has handed himself over wholly to the Lord.
365.1: Kafi: this hymn is to be sung in Asa blended with Raag Kafi. The closing figures count the hymns in Raag Asa so far: 39 by the First Guru and 13 by the Third, 52 in all.
365.2: Sachiar: sach and alaya (abode), the abode of truth, God who ever abides.
ਸਭ ਤੇਰੀ ਤੂੰ ਸਭਨੀ ਧਿਆਇਆ: here ਤੂੰ means you as the object (ਤੈਨੂੰ), and ਸਭਨੀ means by all.
Vijog and sanjog: the powers of God's will that part beings and bring them together.
369.3: Asavari is a raag akin to Asa, and its shabads stand within Raag Asa. Sudhang: in its pure form, sung in the raag's own notes.
369.4: The closing figures total the shabads of Raag Asa so far: 39 by the First Guru, 13 by the Third, 15 by the Fourth, 67 in all.
370.1: The shabad does not name her; in the commentaries she is Maya, who herself speaks in the last two lines. Sati: here, a giver of charity (so the Darpan and the Santhya).
370.2: The commentaries read the household so: the Husband is God, the mother-in-law ignorance (avidya), the sisters-in-law hope and craving, and the elder brother-in-law Dharam Raj.
370.3: In this shabad devotion is a bride: the Guru is her father and the soul her husband. The commentators read her sisters-in-law as hope and craving, and her husband's brothers as the senses (or as greed and pride).

The thirty-two good marks (battih sulakhani): by tradition, the qualities of an ideal wife, among them modesty, compassion, humility and patience. Jaj is a sacred rite (yajna) and kaaj a wedding; at such rites a wife stands beside her husband.
371.1: The woman of this shabad is not named; the commentators read her as Maya, sent into the world to serve, who has made herself mistress of the house of the heart.
372.1: The Banker (Shah) is the Lord, or the Guru through whom he trades; the traders are seekers, and the jewel and the goods are the Name.
373.3: This shabad speaks to the soul-bride, the human being, whose birth stands above all other species. Rahao Dooja: the second Rahao (Pause) of this shabad, which answers the first.
374.1: Iktuke: hymns whose every stanza is a single tuk (one verse in two halves); the figure 2 says that two such hymns follow.
374.2: A seer is an old measure of weight; three (light) seers of grain were held to be a day's food.
378.1: The first six lines counsel the soul; in the last four Nanak prays humbly to God on behalf of all beings.
378.3: Chill and heat (pala, tau) are the two stages of a fever: first the shivering, then the burning. Daki (Sanskrit dakini) is a witch. Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya takes this shabad and the next as thanks for being spared a spreading fever; the Darpan reads the fever and the witch as Maya.
378.5: Cold, hot and earth: water, fire and earth, which take the dead body when it is given to the river, burnt or buried.
378.6: With this shabad the thirty-four shabads of the Fifth Guru in Ghar 2 of Raag Asa are complete; the count of the shabads that follow runs on from them.
381.2: The rebab is a stringed instrument, the pakhavaj a two-headed drum, the taal a pair of cymbals; those who danced in worship danced to them.
381.3: This shabad speaks in paradoxes; the commentators read each image as the changed state of a mind the Guru has given the Amrit of the Naam to drink (the last line). Chandal: a caste held to be lower even than the Shudra.
385.2: In this shabad the garden is the world, its trees and plants are living beings, and the Gardener is the Creator; the pools of poison are Maya's vices, and the Amrit is the Naam.
386.3: Tantra and mantra (tantu, mantu): charms and spells by which people sought to harm others or gain their ends; the charm and the mantra the Guru gives is the Name of the Lord.
390.3: The lines recall an old parable: a man falling into a well caught hold of a rope and hung there, and, tasting the drops of honey that fell from above, forgot that a mouse was gnawing through the rope (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya). The rope is life, the mouse time, and the sweetness the world's pleasures.
390.4: Dutuke: hymns whose every stanza has two tuks (each a verse in two halves); the figure 9 says that nine such hymns begin here.
In this shabad the Guru speaks to the body (ri, a feminine address); the detached one who leaves it is the soul.
390.5: In this shabad he is God and we are the soul, a part of him; once the Guru removes the doubt, the two are one (the last lines).
392.1: Agarak: the chief attendants who walk ahead of their mistress; the commentators read them as lust, anger and the other vices that go before Maya.
392.2: Kaula (Kamala): Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth; here Maya.
393.1: Salagram: a round black stone from the Gandaki river in Nepal, worshipped as a form of Vishnu: it is bathed, offered food, honoured with bell, fly-whisk and incense, and kept in a casket (sampat). In this shabad the Guru names the Lord who pervades all creation as his Salagram.
393.2: In this shabad the road is the journey of life: the water-carrier is the soul-bride caught in vices, the greedy toll-collectors are Jam's messengers, and the caravans that seethe are souls suffering for their deeds.
394.3: The co-wife (saukan): a husband's second wife; here Maya, who holds the house of the soul-bride's heart and stands between her and the Husband Lord.
394.4: The woman of this shabad is Maya.
396.1: By tradition (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya, the Faridkot Teeka) this shabad gives thanks for the birth of (Guru) Hargobind, son of Guru Arjan Dev Ji; by the Santhya the companions' song of joy is the Third Guru's Anand. The Darpan reads the joy of a son's birth as a likeness of the peace that the Guru's refuge brings.
399.2: Bikhli pati (Sanskrit vrishali-pati): the husband or keeper of a dissolute woman, a byword for a debauched man. Amali: one addicted to a drug, who cannot do without it.
400.2: Betel (pan) was chewed by a bride to redden her lips, a part of her adornment for her husband. Madder (majith): a red dye from the root of a plant, a colour that never fades.
400.4: Garah: the nine planets of astrology, held to bring misfortune; sagun and apsagun: good and bad omens, signs read for good or ill luck.
401.1: Sanak and his brothers: Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan and Sanat Kumar, in the Puranas the four sons of Brahma, sages held to remain children for ever.
401.3: The city of Harichand (Harichandauri): a city seen in the sky, a mirage that vanishes as one draws near.
403.1: A muhurat is two gharis. The colocynth (tumma) is a fruit fair to look at but very bitter; swallow-wort (akk) and neem are bywords for bitterness.
406.1: By an old belief (the Faridkot Teeka), in the earlier ages one person's sin brought punishment on his family, town or land as well; the line says that in Kalyug each reaps the fruit of his own deeds alone.
407.6: The nalini is a parrot trap: a reed that turns on a rod set over a bowl of water, with grain on it. When the parrot perches, the reed turns over; seeing the water below, the frightened bird clings to it and so is caught by its own hold.
408.2: Partal: a setting in which the rhythm (taal) changes again and again as the hymn is sung.
408.3: The instruments of the five sounds: the five kinds of instrument (strings, metal, wind, skin drums and pots), an image of full joy within.
409.2: Haan, at the end of the lines of these Asavari shabads, is a syllable sung to the song's measure; it is not rendered.
410.3: Banwari (wearer of the garland of forest flowers, a name of Krishna): in Gurbani, a name of God.
411.2: The yogis' terms: darsan is the garb of a yogi order (yogis call taking the garb taking darsan); bibhut is the ash smeared on the body; nad is their horn; Gagan (the sky) is the highest plane of the mind.
Paaras: the philosopher's stone, held to turn iron into gold at a touch.
413.1: The five: the nearest kin of the one who dies, mother, father, brother, wife and son; some take them to be the five passions, lust and the rest.
Sutak: in Hindu custom, the impurity held to fall on a household for some days after a birth or a death; chhot is defilement by touch.
417.1: This shabad and the next are held to tell of the sack of Saidpur and the slaughter there by Babur's army.
Babarvani: Babur's rule proclaimed. Kuir (kunwar): a prince. Chauka: the purified square of the kitchen, in which Hindus cooked and ate after bathing.
417.2: The Mir is Babur; the Pathans then ruled Hindustan. A torn letter is a summons to death (a letter bearing news of a death was torn at one edge). The Bhattis and the Thakurs are Rajput clans.
418.1: Goil: a pasture to which herdsmen bring their cattle to graze for a season, and then leave.
418.2: Several words of this shabad are of the Lahnda (western Punjabi) speech: maida mine, taida yours, nimhi not, bibha another, hiko the one. Naam, daan, isnaan: remembering the Name, giving, and purity of life.
422.2: Sursari (the river of the gods): the Ganga, which by the Puranas flows from the feet of Vishnu.
426.2: Sabhraaee (sa, with; bhraa, brother): a bride with brothers, and so held in honour in her husband's home.
430.2: The five won over and settled within are the virtues (truth, contentment, compassion, dharma, patience); the five turned away and driven out are the passions (lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride).
Pharhe: gates of planks or bars that close the way into a village or a cattle-pen; muhkam (Persian): firm, strong. Jizya: the poll tax taken from non-Muslims under Muslim rule.
431.1: Murari (the foe of the demon Mur): a name of God.
431.2: Birhare: songs of birha, the pain of separation from the Beloved; these three are sung to the measure (jat) of the chhants.
In the first Birhara, and in the first line of the second, O dear one addresses a dear Sikh; after that, O Beloved addresses God (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya).
432.1: Patti: the wooden slate on which children learn to write their letters.
432.7: Khundkar (Persian khudavandgar): the Lord; Shah Alam: the King of the world.
432.8: The image is the potter's: the Lord has kneaded the clay and shaped the pots (beings); the kiln is the world, and putting the pots in and taking them out is birth and death (the Darpan).
434.2: Madhusudan (the slayer of the demon Madhu): a name of God. The letter Mamma begins both maran (death) and Madhusudan.
434.6: Vasudev: a name of Krishna, son of Vasudeva; in Gurbani it names God, who dwells in all.
434.10: Ayo Angai, Kakhai Ghangai, Riri Lali: names of letters as children recited them in order: a, i, u … ang; k, kh, g, gh, ng; and ri, li, vowels of the Devanagari alphabet (the Darpan).
434.12: Sidhan-ngaiai (siddham, may it be accomplished): the words of blessing the teacher wrote at the head of the slate before the letters (the Darpan).
435.1: The yajman (jajman) is the patron for whom a priest performs rites. The gift taken from the wrong place is, by the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka, the gift taken at the wedding of the patron's daughter, who is to the priest as his own daughter.
435.14: Ram at the end of many lines of these Chhants is a sung word of the measure, a calling on the Lord; it is not rendered.
The seven pools (ਸਾਤ ਸਰ): the five senses, the mind and the intellect.
436.1: The five (ਪੰਚ) here are five virtues: truth, contentment, compassion, dharma and patience.
437.1: The daughter of the ocean (ਸਾਇਰ ਕੀ ਪੁਤ੍ਰੀ): Lakshmi, who in the Puranas rose from the churning of the ocean; here, Maya.
440.1: The closing figures count the Chhants of Raag Asa so far: five by the First Guru and two by the Third, seven in all.
445.1: Satjug, Treta, Duapar and Kalyug are the four ages of the Puranas; dharma, pictured as a bull, stands on four feet in Satjug and loses one in each age after. Kaanh is Krishna, whom the Puranas place in Duapar among the gopis, the herdswomen of Braj.
451.1: Prahlad was the son of the demon king Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu) and held to devotion to God through all his father's torments; in the Puranas, God took the form of Narasimha, the Man-Lion, and killed Harnakhash.
By tradition, the priests of a temple (at Aundha) put Bhagat Namdev, a calico printer by caste, out from before it; he sat singing God's praises at the back, and the temple turned round to face him.
451.2: The chatrik (rain-bird, the pied cuckoo) is held in Indian poetry to drink only the raindrop that falls under the Swati star, and no other water, and to cry out for it.
452.1: The nine treasures (nidhis): by tradition, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; that is, all the riches of the world.
Janji: one of the groom's wedding party (janj); manji: one of the bride's people, the hosts who serve the party.
454.2: The chakvi (ruddy shelduck), parted from her mate at night, waits all night for the sunrise.
Hunters draw the deer at night with the sound of a bell (ghanda hera); the deer gives up its life to that sound.
462.1: A vaar is a hymn of pauris (stanzas); the pauris of this vaar are the First Guru's, and each is preceded by saloks, a few of them the Second Guru's (marked Mahla 2). Tunda Asraja: by tradition a prince whose hand was cut off (tunda, maimed) and who later became a king; the bards sang a vaar of him, and this vaar is set to its tune (dhuni).
463.2: Naah here is the plural of naahu (master), not the negative: barren plants left in a harvested field have no one owner, so anyone who passes may cut them and carry them off.
463.4: True (sacha) here means what truly is and abides: by the Darpan the salok says that God's creation is real, not an illusion, and its order lasting, though its single forms pass away.
463.7: Jajmale (from jazam, leprosy): the leprous; here, those foul with evil deeds.
463.8: Vismaad: the wonder and awe that rise in the mind at the marvels of God's creation.
464.1: Kudrat (Arabic qudrat): power, and the creation in which God's power is at work; Kadir (Qadir) is its Master. The Kateb: the scriptures of the Semitic faiths (the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Quran).
464.2: The bhaur (the black bee) is a name of the soul in Gurbani. Vadda hona (to become great) is an old Punjabi idiom for dying (the Darpan).
464.3: Bhau (fear) in Gurbani is awe of God and of his Hukam, under which all creation keeps its course. Begaar: labour forced from one without pay. A kos is an old measure of distance, about two miles.
464.4: Bajaari (by the Darpan, the raasdharis): troupes who staged the raas in the bazaars for a living, acting out in song and dance the stories of Krishna and the gopis, and of Ram and Sita; the two saloks at 465.2 and 465.3 also speak of the raas. A taka was a coin.
465.5: The salok first tells the ways of the Muslims, the Hindus, the yogis, the givers and the wicked; the Guru's own conclusion is in its last two lines (the Darpan, the Santhya).
466.1: The salok answers a belief held among Muslims, that those whose bodies are burnt burn in the fire of hell (the Darpan).
466.3: Hau (I) and Haumai (I-am-ness): the sense of a self apart from God.
468.2: Kur in this salok is a noun: not a lie told, but what is unreal and passes away, the world's show of illusion; kurai: of the false one, the being caught in it.
468.5: Khumb: the dyer's vat in which cloth is steamed clean before dyeing. Saram here is effort, as in the Saram Khand of the Japji.
469.4: This salok has a Rahao line of its own between its two parts, as a shabad has; it holds the salok's central thought.
469.6: Sabadam here is the way, the duty (dharma), laid down for each.
469.7: Krishna here is a name of the one God.
469.9: Omi (Arabic ummi): unlettered, one who cannot read or write.
470.1: Meru: the mountain at the centre of the earth in the Puranas, and the head bead of a rosary; hence the chief, the best. The body as a chariot with a charioteer is the image of the Katha Upanishad; here the chariot is the bent of people's nature in each age, and the charioteer what leads it.
470.2: The four Vedas are set beside the four ages: the Sama with Satjug, the Rig with Treta, the Yajur with Duapar, the Atharva with Kalyug, each with the name of the Lord that then prevailed: Setambar, Ram, Krishna, Allah. Chandravali: by tradition a gopi of Braj whom Krishna loved. The Parjat: the wish-fulfilling tree of Indra's heaven, which by the Puranas Krishna brought down to earth for his queen Satyabhama. Blue was the dress of the Turk and Pathan rulers of the time.
470.4: The simmal (silk-cotton) tree: tall, straight and bright with red flowers, but its fruit holds nothing to eat, only floss.
470.5: Sandhya: the Brahmin's prayers and rites at dawn, noon and dusk; the three-footed one (traipal) is the Gayatri, the Rig Veda verse in three parts recited at them. The heron stands still in the water as if in trance, but is watching for fish.
471.1: Chaukar: four cowries; the cowrie shell was the smallest money.
471.6: By the commentaries, these lines speak to the Hindu officials of the Muslim rulers, who levied the rulers' tax even on cows and Brahmins and yet kept the rites of purity: the kitchen square plastered with cow-dung, the dhoti, tilak and rosary. Mlechh: impure, alien; the caste Hindus' word for foreigners, here the Muslim rulers.
471.7: The devourers of men: by the commentaries, the officials of the time who preyed on the people by bribes and oppression; those with the knife and the sacred thread are their Hindu clerks. The foreign tongue (abhakhia): Arabic, in which the kalma is recited as the goat is slaughtered halal. Chuli: a handful of water sipped and rinsed in the mouth for ritual purity.
472.2: Pitars: dead forebears. In the shraadh rite, food and goods are given to a Brahmin for them, in the belief that they reach the forebears; the Brahmin who takes them is the go-between (dalal) of this salok.
472.5: In a house under sutak, its food and water are not touched and no rites are performed.
473.3: Bhand is here an old word for woman, not the jester (bhand) of present-day speech.
474.11: Karamat is here a gift of grace, not a miracle: it answers the daat (gift) of the line before.
475.5: Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
475.6: Gun here is a rope: in the dark a rope looks like a snake, and so, through delusion, the world seems to be apart from God. The bimb is the original (the sun or moon) whose reflection falls in the water of the pot; when the pot breaks, the reflection is no longer separate.
476.3: The noseless one (nakti) is shameless Maya, who keeps faith with no one. In the Darpan's reading the five yogis are men given to the five passions, in whose minds Maya sits enthroned as queen; some commentators see here a rite of the left-hand tantrics.
477.1: This hymn speaks in inverted images: Ram has made the impossible happen, and only a rare one understands it. In the Darpan's reading the animals are the mind's old natures (the elephant pride, the ox sloth, the crow cunning, the donkey lust, the buffalo stubbornness), now turned to the Lord's praise; the barren woman's son is the mind born of Maya, setting out to wed an understanding untouched by vice.
477.2: The batua is the yogi's pouch for sacred ash, the adhari his shoulder bag, the mirgani his deerskin seat, and the fahuri the scraper that gathers the ash of his fire-pit. The body's single door is the Tenth Gate, and its nine regions are its nine openings.
478.2: In the Darpan's reading this tells of the state in which Maya's hold (the oil and the wick), its din (the drum) and craving (the fire) come to an end, and the actor (the mind), once made to dance by Maya, comes to rest.
478.4: Hajj: the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca; the Gomti is a river held holy by Hindus, a tirath. Pitambar (clad in yellow) is a name of Vishnu; here, with Pir, it names God himself, whose dwelling, by the Darpan, is the mind.
Sarad (Sharda): Saraswati, the goddess of learning.
479.1: Lapsi: a thin sweet pudding of flour, ghee and sugar; kasar: flour roasted in ghee with sugar. Food offered before an idol is afterwards eaten by its priests.
480.1: Qazi: the Muslim judge, who also taught the law of Islam. Roza, namaz and kalma: the fast, the daily prayer and the creed; the musalla is the prayer mat.

Satar: seventy, as elsewhere in Kabir's verse (ਸਤਰਿ ਸੈਇ, ਸਤਰਿ ਦੋਇ); seventy Kaabas, that is, many (the Shabdarth), the greatest Kaaba (the Santhya). The Darpan reads it as the Arabic sitr (a veil): the hidden Kaaba.
480.2: The yogis speak of nectar that drips from the Gagan and of the sound (nad) heard within in deep meditation. The ten fastenings: by the Santhya, the ten vital airs (pranas) that hold the body together.
By Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya and the Faridkot Teeka the shabad tells of a body the soul has left; the Darpan reads it as the mind that has died to the body's attachments.
481.2: Ravan, the demon king of Lanka in the Ramayana, whose fort the ocean ringed like a moat; by tradition he held the gods in his service.
Loi: by the Darpan, people, the world (ਰੇ is the masculine address; the feminine is ਰੀ); by tradition, Loi was also the name of Kabir's wife.
481.3: This shabad speaks in paradoxes; the commentators read them as the soul, pure as it came from God, fallen under the sway of the mind and the senses: by the Darpan the soul was first pure (puut) and afterwards came under Maya (maai); the guru is the soul and the disciple the mind, the lion the soul and the cows the senses.
The closing line counts Bhagat Kabir Ji's shabads in Raag Asa so far: thirteen Chaupade and nine Panchpade, twenty-two in all.
482.1: In this shabad Kabir speaks as a bride wedded to God. The bhavar (laavan) are the rounds that bride and groom walk at the wedding; the vedi is the square set up for them to sit in. The three hundred and thirty million are, by tradition, the gods.
482.2: The soul speaks as a bride in her in-laws' house. By the Darpan the mother-in-law is Maya, the father-in-law the love of the body, the husband's elder brother death, his sister the senses and his younger brother discernment; the stepfather is the body, and the elder brother, with whom she was in the womb, the knowledge of God.
482.3: In this shabad Kabir speaks to a Brahmin; in the lines of the cows and the herdsmen, the herdsmen are the Brahmins, who call themselves the keepers of others.
482.4: ਜਗਿ ਜੀਵਨੁ in the first line (two words) is life in the world; ਜਗਜੀਵਨੁ in the last line (one word) is the Life of the world, God.
482.5: The image is a dancer's: in birth after birth the soul took many guises and danced (at Maya's bidding) with its thread, string and drum (the Darpan: the thread and the string of attachment).
483.3: Dupade: hymns of two stanzas each. The swan (hans) is held to pick out pearls and to part milk from water; here it is the soul that has gained the discernment to know the Lord.
483.4: By the Darpan the two brides are two states of the mind (the Santhya: kumati and sumati, the evil and the good understanding): the first proud and turned to Maya, the second humble and turned to God.
484.1: By the Darpan the whole shabad is Kabir's own: the bride is his soul, once fond of wealth and now Ram's handmaid, the little son his mind, and the shaven-headed ones the holy men of his company. By an old tradition (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya), the first four lines are his mother's complaint and the last two his answer.
484.2: The bride is the soul; her veil, by the Darpan, is her hiding her face from the Husband Lord. The damri was the smallest coin.
484.3: Karvat (the saw): by the Santhya, a saw at Kashi (and Prayag) under which people had their bodies cut, hoping for liberation.
484.4: The weaver's terms: the warp (tana) is the threads stretched lengthwise; the karghah, by the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka, the comb of the loom; the saath, the shuttles; the paai jor, the pair of treadles the weaver works with his feet. The Weaver is God; Kabir himself was a weaver.
484.5: By an old belief, whoever dies at Banaras (Kashi) is liberated, and whoever dies at Magahar is born again as a donkey.
485.2: Bithal (Vitthal): Namdev's name for God; in this shabad the image is called the Thakur, and the all-pervading Lord Bithal. By tradition, forty-two lakh of the eighty-four lakh species of beings live in water.
485.3: Namdev speaks in the terms of his trade (printing and sewing cloth): the yardstick, the scissors, the dyeing vat, the needle and the thread. Paati: lineage, the clan within a caste.
485.4: Singhach bhojan: the lion's food, a living got by force and deceit. Dagra: by the Darpan a Marathi word for stone, the stone-hearted; the Santhya also reads it as the path, or as deceiver.
486.2: Each creature dies through one sense: the deer through hearing (the hunter's bell), the fish through taste (the bait), the bumblebee through smell (shut in the lotus), the moth through sight (the flame), and the elephant through touch (lured by lust into a pit). Man has all five.
486.3: Several words of this shabad are Marathi: chi, cho, cha (of), majhai (to me), olhag (a servant), olhagani (service).
487.1: This verse holds two shabads; the second begins at Mati ko putra, with its own Rahao.
By tradition the boy Namdev set milk before the Lord and would not rise until the Lord drank it.
487.3: This shabad is the Fifth Guru's, set among Bhagat Dhanna Ji's; it tells what moved Dhanna to devotion.
488.3: Cranes come to the plains in Katik (October to November) and fly off when the season ends; in the Rahao they are the restless senses. Forests catch fire in Chet (March to April), and lightning flashes in Savan (July to August): each comes in its season and is gone.
The boatmen: by the Darpan, the great leaders of the world; by Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya, the souls that steer the boat of the body.
489.1: In temple worship, sandalwood is ground on a stone (ursa) with water into a paste, saffron (kungu) is mixed in, and the image is marked with it; here each of these becomes inward.
489.2: In the Puranas Brahma was born of a lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel, and went down its stalk to find where it began, but found no end.
The Siddhas are yogis held to have reached perfection. Murari (the foe of the demon Mur): a name of God.
490.2: Ji at the end of the opening lines is an address of affection to the listener, rendered O brother. The Simritis and the Shastras: the Hindu books of law and of philosophy.
490.3: The Tenth Gate (dasam duar): the inner door beyond the body's nine openings, where the soul meets God.
By Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya the Guru here tells his own experience: through the Guru, the disciple became the Guru. The Darpan reads it of anyone who takes the Guru's refuge.
491.1: Haumai (I-am-ness): the sense of a self apart from God. Dubidha (duality): the divided mind, which loves another besides God. Dharam Raj judges each soul by its deeds.
491.2: Paaras: the philosopher's stone, held to turn iron into gold at a touch.
491.3: Panchpade (panch, five; pad, stanza): hymns of five stanzas. Kashi (Banaras): the city on the Ganges held most holy, a seat of learning; the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage are the tiraths held most holy in India.
The self made of the five elements (panch bhu atma): by Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya and the Faridkot Teeka, the mind; the Darpan reads it as the mind fallen under the five (lust, anger and the rest).
492.2: This shabad is also in Rehras (Ang 10), with a few small differences of wording. Rahraas: the provisions for a journey; for the journey of life, the Lord's praise. The evening bani, Rehras, takes its name from it.
492.3: Kaula (Kamala): Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. Riddhis and siddhis: wealth and the miraculous powers of yoga.
The crow feeds on filth; the swan (hans) is held to pick out pearls and to part milk from water.
493.3: Nirban (nirvana): free of desire; the nirban pad is the state in which desire is extinguished.
495.1: The crane (koonj) flies hundreds of kos in winter, leaving her young behind.
The treasures: by tradition, the nine treasures (nidhis). Of the eighteen siddhis, eight (anima, laghima and the rest) are the best known.
495.2: The six rites (khat karam): the six duties of a Brahmin: studying and teaching the Vedas, performing and officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving gifts.
496.1: The chatrik (rain-bird, the pied cuckoo) is held in Indian poetry to drink only the raindrop that falls under the Swati star, and no other water.
498.1: Namdev, Trilochan, Kabir and Ravidas are Bhagats whose hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib; Ravidas was of the leather-working caste.
498.5: The three gods: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. Thirty-three crore (330 million): the number of the gods in Puranic tradition.
500.2: Yakshas and Kinnars: classes of demigods in the Puranas.
500.5: By tradition (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya) this shabad gives thanks for the healing of (Guru) Hargobind, son of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, from smallpox in his childhood.
501.1: Sridhar (he who holds Sri, Lakshmi): a name of Vishnu; in Gurbani, a name of God.
502.1: The three fevers: adhi (ills of the mind), biadhi (ills of the body) and upadhi (troubles and calamities that come from without).
503.1: The five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Trihdas: the three (trih) are the qualities of Maya, rajas, sattva and tamas; the ten (das) are the organs of sense and of action.
Vasudev (who dwells in all) and Banwali (who wears the garland of the forest): names of Krishna, which in Gurbani name God.

The tree with its root above and branches below is the Gita's image of the world (15.1): a fig tree (ashvattha) rooted above, spreading downward, whose leaves are the Vedas. The Paarjat (Parijata) is a tree of Indra's heaven which, in the Puranas, rose from the churning of the ocean and grants every wish.
503.2: Ai ji: a respectful call, O dear one; in these hymns it is addressed now to the listener, now to the Guru, now to God, as the line shows.
Sunn (the void): the state before creation, when there was nothing but God.
506.1: Shiv and Shakti: here Shiv is the Lord, the source of good, and Shakti is Maya; the house of Shiv is wakefulness in God, the house of Shakti the sleep of Maya.
The four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth.
506.2: Sanak and Sanandan: two of the four sons of Brahma in the Puranas (Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan and Sanat Kumar), sages held to remain children for ever; Narad is a sage of the Puranas, a devotee of Vishnu.
Prahlad, son of the demon king Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu), held to devotion to God through all his father's torments, and God saved him.
508.1: Narhar (Narasimha, the Man-Lion in whose form, in the Puranas, God saved Prahlad), Keshav (of the beautiful hair) and Dharnidhar are names of Vishnu in the Puranas; in Gurbani they are names of the one God.
Param Hans (the supreme swan): of old, the name of a soul of the highest order.
508.2: A vaar is a hymn of pauris (stanzas); the pauris of this vaar are the Third Guru's, and each is preceded by two saloks, all the Third Guru's but one (Bhagat Kabir Ji's). Sikandar and Birahim (Ibrahim): by tradition, two chiefs of one clan whose fight the bards sang as a vaar; this vaar is to be sung to its tune (dhuni).
509.4: Turiya (the fourth state): the spiritual state beyond the three qualities of Maya.
510.3: Gararu: one who knows the spell that draws out snake venom, named after Garuda, the bird who is the enemy of snakes.
510.4: A dhadhi is a bard who sings a patron's praise (a vaar) at his door; here, the devotee who sings the Lord's praise.
512.2: Binde: knows (Sanskrit vid, to know); by the word's own sense, a Brahmin is one who knows Brahm.
513.3: Jangams are Shaiva mendicants who go about ringing bells; sannyasis are ascetics who have renounced home.
513.5: Maaran: in the physicians' usage, the herb that kills a poison such as arsenic (reduces it to ash) and makes it harmless.
514.2: Waah Waah: the cry of wonder at something marvellous; in these saloks, the praise of God, for which no words are enough.
516.3: Gujri: a woman of the Gujjar people, herders and sellers of milk, whose caste was counted low.
516.5: Partial incarnations (ansa avtar): in the Puranas, incarnations held to bear only a portion of the divine power.
517.1: The high house is the cloud: seeing the clouds, the farmer raises the embankments of his field so that the rain-water stays in it. Mahal: wife, woman.
517.6: Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
518.4: The Kateb: the scriptures of the Semitic faiths (the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Quran).
520.10: Jambur: pincers with which flesh was torn from the body in torture.
524.4: Kapi is read, as the traditional commentators read it, as the oil-presser's ox, which circles the press all night and gets nowhere.
525.3: Malaya: the hills of South India famed for sandalwood, round whose trees snakes are said to coil. By tradition, poison and Amrit both came out of the ocean when it was churned.
526.1: Trilochan speaks in the terms of the belief, common in his day, that the last thought at death shapes the next birth. Pitambar (clad in yellow): a name of Krishna, which he uses for the Lord.
526.2: Jaidev writes in a language close to Sanskrit, and its case endings decide the sense: jasamarnen is by remembering it, and jogen, jagen, daanen and tapsaa are by yoga, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity.
528.2: Chhaka 1: the first set of six shabads; the count is written after the shabad's numbers.
531.3: Pooja, archa (offering sandal-paste and the like), bandan, moorat and dhyan are the terms of image-worship; here each is given to serving the Guru's feet and the company of the Sants.
531.4: The four padaarath: dharam (righteousness), arth (wealth), kaam (fulfilment of desire) and mokh (liberation), held to be the four aims of life.
532.2: ਸਉਤੁ (Sanskrit sa-putra) means one blessed with a son: the Lord's servant is a worthy son who brings honour to the Creator, his Father.
537.1: Most words of this hymn take the added ending -ria for the measure (sangria for sang, the company; mohria for moh, attachment; sahajria for sahaj); the sense is that of the plain word.
537.3: Ram at the end of many lines of these Chhants is a sung word of the measure, a calling on the Lord; it is not rendered.
O my dear soul (meri jindurie): the Guru calls on his own soul with affection; the call comes in nearly every line of these Chhants.
The Anhad (anāhata, unstruck) Shabad is the sound made by no striking: the divine music that sounds unbroken through all creation.
538.1: The pigeon: lured by grain scattered under the fowler's net, it walks in and is caught of its own accord.
539.1: The nine treasures (nidhis): by tradition, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; that is, all the riches of the world.
541.1: Chhaka 1: one set of six; the figure marks the close of these six Chhants of the Fourth Guru.
543.1: Murari (the foe of the demon Mur): a name of God.
546.1: Dharam Raj judges each soul by its deeds.
The red-hot pillars: a torment of hell told in the Puranas, in which the sinner is made to embrace a pillar of glowing metal.
547.2: The city of Harichand (Harichandauri): a city seen in the sky, a mirage that vanishes as one draws near.
The closing figures count the Fifth Guru's Chhants in Raag Bihagra: three in Ghar 1 and six in Ghar 2, nine in all.
550.6: The commentaries read this image differently: in the Darpan the tree is the world, its fruit attachment to Maya, and the two birds the Gurmukh and the manmukh; in Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya the tree is the body, its fruit the Lord's essence, and the two birds the soul and the Supreme Soul, as in the two birds on one tree of the Rig Veda (1.164.20) and the Mundaka Upanishad.
553.1: Mardana: Bhai Mardana, Guru Nanak Dev Ji's companion who played the rebab. These three saloks are the Guru's own (the first two carry the signature Nanak), spoken to Mardana.
555.6: Thirty-six ages: a figure for the countless ages before creation. Sunn (the void): the state before creation, when there was nothing but God.
556.3: Jinn: in Muslim belief, unseen beings made of fire, often thought to do harm.
556.4: Narad: a sage of the Puranas who, by tradition, laid down the rites of image worship.
556.8: Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
557.3: Saavan: the month of the rains (July–August), in Punjabi poetry the season of longing for an absent husband. The chooda: the red bangles a bride puts on at her wedding.
559.3: Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu are the three gods of the Puranas; the commentators read Kisan (Krishna) here as Vishnu, of whom Krishna is held to be an incarnation. Tamas: of the three qualities of Maya, the one of darkness and inertia.
566.1: Krishna's garland (ਕ੍ਰਿਸਨ ਮਾਲਾ): the garland of forest flowers (Vaijayanti) that Krishna wears. The heron, standing still as if in meditation while it watches for fish, is the image of the hypocrite; the swan, of the pure soul.
567.1: Ram at the end of many lines of these Chhants is a sung word of the measure, a calling on the Lord; it is not rendered.
Muiye (literally, O dead one) is a Punjabi word with which women address one another, here fondly; it is rendered dear one.
569.1: The nine treasures (nidhis): by tradition, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; that is, all the riches of the world.
575.1: Ghorian: the wedding songs that the groom's sisters and the women of the house sing as he mounts the mare to ride out for his wedding; in these two chhants the human body is the mare.
576.1: The unstruck (Anhad) trumpets: the divine music, made by no striking, that sounds unbroken within.
578.2: Alahniyan: the dirges women sing together over the dead, praising the departed and beating their breasts in time. In their measure the Guru teaches acceptance of the Lord's will and his praise in place of wailing.
The cup (paai): the bowl of a water-clock, with a small hole in its bottom; floating on water it slowly fills and sinks. The full cup is the measure of a life run out.
580.1: The four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth. The tongues (bani): the speech of beings.
The nine doors: the nine openings of the body (two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth and the two lower openings).
The true words: the call Ram naam sat hai (the Lord's Name is true), raised as the bier is carried.
581.1: The -va at the end of lines here is a sung syllable of the dirge's measure; it is not rendered.
581.2: Saha: the day fixed for a wedding, when the bride leaves her parents' home and which cannot be put off; here the appointed hour of leaving the world.
585.1: The pauris of Vadhans ki Vaar are the Fourth Guru's; each is preceded by saloks, most of them the Third Guru's. Lalan Behlima: by tradition Lalan and Behlima, two Rajput chiefs of the Kangra country; in a drought Lalan took water from Behlima's canal, promising a sixth of his crop, and broke his word; the bards sang their fight as a vaar, and this vaar is to be sung to its tune (dhuni). Vadh hans (great swan) in the first salok is the raag's own name.
588.4: Kalyug: in the reckoning of the Puranas, the fourth and darkest of the world's four ages, held to be the present one.
589.1: Marjeevra is also the word for the pearl-diver, who plunges into the sea and comes up with pearls.
591.3: Prahlad, son of the demon king Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu), held to devotion to God through all his father's torments. Janak, king of Mithila and father of Sita, is remembered as a sage who stayed detached while he ruled. Basisht (Vasishtha) was the sage who was guru to Ram's house; his teaching to Ram is told in the Yoga Vasishtha.
594.7: Nisal: lying at ease, the body loosened and the limbs stretched out; that is, hoping in no one else and fearing no one else.
Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
596.1: Chautuke: hymns whose every stanza has four tuks (lines).
596.2: Dutuke: hymns whose every stanza has two tuks (each a verse in two halves).
597.2: The sixty-eight places of pilgrimage are the tiraths held most holy in India.
598.3: Sohang (so-ham, he am I): the awareness of the one who has merged in God that the soul is not apart from him.
601.2: Prahlad was the son of the demon king Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu) and held to devotion to God through all his father's torments; in the Puranas, God took the form of Narasimha, the Man-Lion, and tore Harnakhash apart with his claws.
602.1: The Anhad (unstruck) Shabad is the divine sound that rings within without being struck.
603.1: The three qualities (gunas) of Maya: rajas, sattva and tamas. The fourth (chautha) is the fourth state (turiya), beyond them.
603.2: Sandhya: the Brahmin's prayers and rites at dawn, noon and dusk; tarpan: offering water to the ancestors and the gods; the Gayatri: the Rig Veda verse recited at them.
604.2: Muhahu: from the mouth; the ending -ahu means from, as in dhurahu, from the very source.
605.2: Tank: a small weight of four mashas; in God's scales the whole earth weighs no more than that.
606.2: Kanh (Krishna), in the Puranas, grew up among the cowherds of Braj, grazing cows in the forest and playing the flute; the gopis were the cowherds' women.
Kuvaliapir: the elephant that Kans set upon the boy Krishna at Mathura; Krishna slew it, and Chandur, Kans's wrestler, the demon Keshi, and Kans, his uncle, himself.
608.1: Tituke: hymns whose every stanza has three lines.
Raja here is not king but a verb: rajan, I am sated.
609.2: Water, dogs, ashes: the three ways a dead body is disposed of: cast into a river, left to the dogs, or burnt to ash.
611.3: In the first two stanzas the seeker pleads with a friend, a fellow disciple of the Guru; the last two stanzas give the answer.
612.2: Sukhmana: in the yogis' teaching, the central channel of the subtle body, said to open in the highest bliss; the inverted lotus is the heart turned away from God. The line uses these figures for the peace found through the Guru.
617.1: Dupade (du, two; pad, stanza): hymns of two stanzas.
617.2: The four great gifts (padaarath): dharam, arth, kaam and mokh, the four aims of life: righteousness, wealth, fulfilment of desire and liberation. The nine treasures (nidhis): by tradition, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; that is, all the riches of the world.
619.1: By tradition (the Faridkot Teeka, the Shabdarth), Guru Arjan Dev Ji uttered this shabad and several after it in thanks for the recovery from fever of his son, the child (Guru) Hargobind.
623.1: The pool of Ramdas (Ramdas Sarovar): the sacred pool at Amritsar, begun by Guru Ram Das Ji and named after him; Ramdas also means the servants of Ram, so the pool is read too as the Saadh Sangat.
624.2: Bithal (Vitthal): a name of God, the One who stands beyond Maya.
Rahao Dooja: the second Rahao (Pause) of this shabad; in it the longing of the first Rahao is fulfilled.
627.4: Sitala is smallpox, which people took to be the wrath of the goddess Sitala.
631.4: Tirath: here the holy, who are themselves the true places of pilgrimage; the like line of the next shabad has gur janu, the Guru, in its place.
632.1: Ganika: a courtesan, saved by teaching a parrot to say Ram. Dhru: the child prince who, slighted by his stepmother, gave himself to devotion and was given an unmoving place as the Pole Star. Gaj: in the Bhagavat Purana, an elephant seized in the water by a crocodile; when his strength failed he called on the Lord and was set free. Ajamal: a fallen Brahmin, saved when at death he called on his son Narayan.
634.2: Sunn Samadhi: absorption in Sunn, the stillness where no worldly thought stirs.
Bhai: in the lines that speak to God as you, it is a loving address to him, O dear one; in the other lines, O brother.
637.1: Riddhis and siddhis: wealth and the miraculous powers of yoga.
638.1: Burnt iron (manur): iron burnt to slag. Paaras: the philosopher's stone, held to turn iron into gold at a touch.
640.1: In the Rahao and in the lines that speak to God as you, O Beloved addresses God; in the other lines, as the Darpan reads them, O dear one addresses the listener.
641.1: Nivli: a hatha yoga practice in which the belly muscles are rolled to cleanse the bowels; bhuangam: by the Darpan, the serpent-shaped kundalini channel along the spine, up which the yogis draw the breath. The five: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
Karpati: one who uses his hands as his only bowl. The saw (karvat): by the Darpan, Shiva's saw at Banaras, under which some had themselves cut, hoping to reach Shiva's heaven.

The six rites (khat karam): the six duties of a Brahmin: studying and teaching, performing and officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving gifts. The eighty-four postures (asanas) are the sitting postures of hatha yoga; the Siddhs are yogis perfected in them.
642.1: The pauris of Sorath ki Vaar are the Fourth Guru's; each is preceded by saloks, the first the First Guru's and most of them the Third Guru's. Sorath in the first two saloks is the raag's own name.

The in-laws' home and the parents' home: the world hereafter and this world. The husband's younger and elder brothers (devar, jeth) are, by the Darpan, the vices, lust and the rest; the mother-in-law (sasu) is Maya.
645.5: Mudavani: a thing sealed, a riddle; the riddle here is that the plate's three things are not named. The Fifth Guru's Mundavani at the close of the Granth opens with the same plate and names them: sat, santokh and vichar (truth, contentment and reflection).
648.7: Hasan: by the Darpan, the dry well in which the Parsis lay their dead, to be eaten by vultures.
650.4: A dhadhi is a bard who sings a patron's praise (a vaar) at his door; here, the devotee who sings the Lord's praise. Kavla (Kamala): Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth; here Maya.
651.2: Kalyug: in the reckoning of the Puranas, the fourth and darkest of the world's four ages, held to be the present one.
653.9: Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
654.1: Kaparis: an order of ascetics who wore a cloak of patched rags. Kedar (Kedarnath): a shrine of Shiva high in the Himalayas, held to be a place of pilgrimage.
654.2: The nalini is a parrot trap: a reed that turns on a rod set over a bowl of water, with grain on it. When the parrot perches, the reed turns over; seeing the water below, the frightened bird clings to it and so is caught by its own hold.
654.3: Khalsa: land held directly by the sovereign, under no lesser lord; here, free of Jam's ledger, belonging to the Lord alone.
655.3: These lines speak in paradoxes: as the Darpan reads them, by wearing away the self the soul (the saffron, the son) becomes one with God (the sandalwood, the Father) and brings him forth within; the ever-wandering mind comes to rest.
657.1: Ho, sung at the end of the lines, is a call that carries the tune; it is not rendered.

The ocean bridged, Sita brought back, Lanka given to Bhabhikhan (Vibhishan): in the Ramayana, Ram's bridge across the ocean to Lanka, Sita won back from Ravan, and Ravan's brother, who took refuge with Ram, made king of Lanka.
658.3: Surtar: the trees of Indra's heaven that, in the Puranas, grant every wish; Chintamani: the jewel that, by tradition, grants whatever is wished for in the mind; Kamdhenu: the cow of heaven in the Puranas, held to grant whatever is asked of her.
The thirty-four letters: the letters of the alphabet; all that is written in words.
658.4: The chakor: a bird said in Indian lore to gaze at the moon all night long.
659.1: Raja and Chand are addresses to God, O King and O Moon, not the name Ramchandra.
659.3: Banwari (wearer of the garland of forest flowers, a name of Krishna): in Gurbani, a name of God.
660.1: Chaupade (chau, four; pad, stanza): hymns of four stanzas.
Each of the four stanzas of this shabad is followed by a Rahao line of its own.
660.2: To die while alive: to die to Haumai (ego) and to worldly desire while still living in the body.
661.2: Dubidha (duality): the divided mind, which loves another besides God.
The True Guru's form (moorat): in Gurbani the Guru's form is his Word, the Shabad (the Darpan: the Guru's spiritual form, his Bani).
662.2: The three writs: by the Darpan, the records of deeds done under the three qualities (gunas) of Maya, rajas, tamas and sattva.
Qazi: the Muslim judge, who also taught the law of Islam.
662.3: Kalyug: in the reckoning of the Puranas, the fourth and darkest of the world's four ages, held to be the present one.
Padam asan: the lotus posture of yoga, sitting cross-legged with each foot upon the opposite thigh.
Mlechh: impure, alien; the caste Hindus' word for foreigners, here the Muslim rulers of the time. Varna: the four caste orders of Hindu society.
The eight (asht saaj): works of grammar; by the Faridkot Teeka the eight grammars composed by the rishis, by the Darpan works such as Panini's Ashtadhyayi (eight chapters).
663.1: Aarti is the worship in which a platter of lamps, incense and flowers is waved before an image; in this shabad all of nature performs the Creator's aarti. Malaanalo (malaya + anila, wind) is the fragrant breeze from the sandalwood hills of Malaya in the south of India; the fly-whisk (chaur) is waved over one who is revered.
The Anhad (anāhata, unstruck) Shabad is the sound made by no striking: the divine music that sounds unbroken through all creation.
The saaring (papiha, the rain-bird) is said to drink only drops of rain, and to keep calling out for them.
664.1: Haumai (I-am-ness): the sense of a self apart from God.
665.3: Bairag: in Gurbani often a loving longing for the Lord, not only renunciation of the world.

The four ages: Satjug, Treta, Duapar and Kalyug of the Puranic count; that is, at all times. The Siddhas are yogis held to have reached perfection; the seekers (sadhiks), those who practise the disciplines of yoga.
666.3: Banwari (wearer of the garland of forest flowers, a name of Krishna): in Gurbani, a name of God.
668.2: Chitr and Gupt are, by tradition, the two recorders at Dharam Raj's court who write down the deeds of every being.
Shiv here means the auspicious One, the giver of good, not the god Shiva.
668.3: Paaras: the philosopher's stone, held to turn iron into gold at a touch; sandalwood is held to make the trees near it fragrant. Murari (the foe of the demon Mur): a name of God.
The nine and the six: by the Darpan and the Shabdarth, the nine Sanskrit grammars and the six Shastras (schools of philosophy).
669.2: The Buddhas: the enlightened, like Gautam Buddha; the thirty-three crore: the gods as tradition counts them.
670.2: Girdhari: the upholder of the mountain, a name of Krishna; here the one Lord.
670.3: The elephant is said to be caught by a paper she-elephant set over a covered pit; the deer, spellbound by the hunter's bell (ghanda hera), is killed.
673.1: Saakat (Sanskrit shakta): a worshipper of Shakti (Maya); in Gurbani, one cut off from God and lost in Maya.
The city of Harichand (Harichandauri): a city seen in the sky, a mirage that vanishes as one draws near.
675.1: Ketu: a banner; it is also the name of an ill-omened planet of astrology.
677.2: Narayan: a name of Vishnu (he whose dwelling is the waters); in Gurbani the one Lord.
679.2: Dupade (du, two; pad, stanza): hymns of two stanzas.
679.3: The nine treasures (nidhis): by tradition, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; that is, all the riches of the world. Riddhis and siddhis: wealth and the miraculous powers of yoga.
680.5: Damodar (he whose waist was bound with a cord: the child Krishna) is a name of Vishnu and Krishna in the Puranas; in Gurbani it is a name of the one God.
681.2: Mrig trishna (the deer's thirst): the mirage of water on hot sand, which the thirsty deer runs after.
682.3: Baikunth: in the Puranas, the heaven of Vishnu.
682.4: Svasti: well-being; bivastha: state. Madhyant (madhya, middle; ant, end): from the middle to the end, that is, always.
683.2: Partal: a setting in which the rhythm (taal) changes again and again as the hymn is sung.
685.3: Ashtapadi (ashta, eight; pad, stanza): a hymn of about eight stanzas.

The lake and the swan: in Indian poetry the swan lives on the lake Mansarovar and feeds on pearls, and the crane, white outside but lying in wait for fish, is the image of the hypocrite; here the lake is the Guru and the swan the Guru's Sikh.
Sunn Mandal: the realm of Sunn, the stillness where no stirring of Maya arises. The Naths: the perfected masters of the yogis, such as Gorakhnath.
The fourth state (turiya): the spiritual state beyond Maya's three qualities.
686.2: The four ashrams: in Hindu custom the four stages of life, the student (brahmacharya), the householder (grihasth), the forest-dweller (vanaprasth) and the renunciant (sannyas), each with its own duties.
Rahao Dooja: the second Rahao (Pause) of this ashtapadi, which answers the prayer of the first.
687.1: Chhant: a song of longer stanzas.

The ten parbs (das purab): by the Darpan, the ten holy days of the calendar, such as the new moon, the full moon, the first day of the month (sangrand) and the eclipses of sun and moon. Dasahara (das, ten; hara, taking away), the day held to take away ten sins, is the tenth of the bright half of Jeth, kept as the birthday of the Ganga.
Beni (Triveni): the meeting of the Ganga, the Jamuna and the Saraswati at Prayag, counted a great place of holy bathing.
688.1: Many lines of these Chhants close with ਜੀਉ (jeeo), a word of loving address that rounds off the line; it adds nothing to the sense.
689.1: The akk (swallow-wort) is a low wild shrub; its shade is scant and soon gone.
Pir dhan bhavai ta pir bhavai nari: pir with aunkar (ਪਿਰੁ) is the subject, the Husband who is dear to the bride; pir without it (ਪਿਰ) means to the Husband.
691.2: Sanak and Sanand (Sanandan): two of the four sons of Brahma in the Puranas (Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan and Sanat Kumar), sages held to remain children for ever. Shesh Nag: the thousand-headed serpent of the Puranas, held to utter a new Name of God with every tongue.
Hanuman is the servant of Ram; Garur (Garuda), the king of birds, is the mount of Vishnu.
692.2: Kashi (Banaras), Shiva's city, was believed to free whoever died there, and Magahar to send whoever died there into birth as a donkey; to break this belief, Kabir left Kashi in old age to live and die at Magahar.
692.4: Ajamal: a fallen Brahmin, saved when at death he called on his son Narayan. Gaj: in the Bhagavat Purana, an elephant seized in the water by a crocodile; when his strength failed he called on the Lord and was set free. Ganika: a courtesan, saved by teaching a parrot to say Ram.
692.5: Markandeya: a sage of the Puranas, held to have lived an exceedingly long life, who yet spent it all in a hut of straw.

The Kauravs: in the Mahabharata, the sons of King Dhritarashtra, Duryodhan the eldest, slain by the Pandavas in the war at Kurukshetra. A jojan (yojana) is about four kos; the royal canopy (chhatar) is the sign of sovereignty.

Durbasa: a sage quick to anger and to curse. Youths of the Yadavs (Krishna's clan) dressed a boy as a pregnant woman and asked him in mockery what she would bear; by his curse the whole Yadav clan fell to fighting among themselves and perished.
693.1: The ten: the ten senses, of perception and of action; the five: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Satar doi (seventy and two): by yogic lore, the seventy-two thousand channels (nadis) of the body.
693.2: The chakvi (ruddy shelduck), parted from her mate at night, waits all night for the sunrise.
693.3: In this shabad Namdev uses Marathi and Sanskrit words: che (of), pundarak (the white lotus), krisna (the Lord who draws all), pursabira (the Purakh became manifest), pursadamra (from the Purakh, Maya), pindhi (the pots of a Persian wheel), naiya (the leader, the Lord), ala (the house, the world's snare).
694.4: The eighteen loads: all plant life; an old belief holds that one leaf of every kind of tree and plant, weighed together, comes to eighteen bhaar (an old measure of weight).

Das atha (ten and eight): the eighteen Puranas; athsathe: the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage, the tiraths held most holy in India; the four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth. Bhog: the food set before the deity in worship.
695.1: The Puranic stories: the moon bears a stain for its misdeed, by the curse of the sage Gautam; it sits on Shiva's brow, and Krishna, Vishnu's incarnation, was born in the lunar line. Arun, the dawn, Garur's elder brother and the sun's charioteer, was born lame. Shiva cut off one of Brahma's heads, and the skull clung to his hand until it fell away at the tirath of Kapal-mochan. The ocean yielded fourteen jewels when it was churned, and is salt still. Hanuman, for all his service to Ram, had only a loincloth.
Re (masculine) and ri (feminine) are words of address.
695.2: Kamla pati (Lakshmi's husband): a name of Vishnu; here the one Lord.
695.3: Jangams are Shaiva mendicants who go about ringing bells.
695.4: Aarta (Sanskrit arta): afflicted, in need; it is not aarti. Sat si: (a field) ploughed seven times.
